# The Strange Comfort of Uncertainty

I've been thinking lately about how we're all collectively pretending that certainty is a normal state of being. We're not, and it never was, but we've become remarkably skilled at the pretense.

Walk into any coffee shop in any major city and you'll see people hunched over laptops, phones glowing in the dark, their faces illuminated by carefully curated versions of their lives. Everyone appears to know exactly where they're going, what they're doing, and why it matters. LinkedIn profiles read like résumés for a life well-planned. Social media streams chronicle the highlights of journeys that seem preordained, as though their narrators simply executed a master plan they'd formulated years ago.

But here's what I think: nobody actually knows what they're doing. We're all just figuring it out as we go, and the ones who seem most confident are usually just better at committing to their own narratives.

I find this comforting, actually.

There's a strange freedom in accepting that uncertainty isn't a temporary condition—something you pass through on your way to understanding—but rather the default state of human existence. We're meaning-making creatures adrift in a fundamentally ambiguous universe, and we've invented countless systems to organize that chaos. Religion, science, philosophy, psychology, social structures, routines. These are all magnificent human creations, but they're creations nonetheless. The universe itself doesn't come pre-loaded with meaning or purpose. We pour that in.

What would it mean to actually embrace this? Not in some nihilistic "nothing matters so why bother" way, but in a genuinely liberatory sense?

I think about the people who seem most alive—not the most successful, necessarily, but the most genuinely engaged with their own existence. They tend to be the ones who've made peace with not knowing. They ask better questions than they answer. They're curious in the way children are curious, except they've also accumulated enough experience to recognize patterns and understand context. They're not waiting to feel ready before they do things. They understand that readiness is mostly a myth, that every meaningful thing you do will involve some degree of stepping forward into fog.

The irony is that we build entire industries around the promise of certainty. Self-help books, coaching programs, productivity systems, investment advisors—they all traffic in the fantasy that if you just follow these steps, absorb this knowledge, implement this framework, you can reduce life to something manageable and knowable. And some of it helps! I'm not cynical about all of it. But the underlying pitch is always the same: let me sell you a map to a territory that doesn't actually exist.

What strikes me most is how exhausting the performance of certainty must be. To maintain that facade constantly—in your professional life, your romantic relationships, your friendships, your relationship to yourself—requires an enormous amount of energy. You have to keep editing. You have to pretend that the doubts don't exist, or that you've overcome them, or that you never had them in the first place. You're constantly scanning for inconsistencies in your own narrative, making sure everything aligns.

I wonder what would happen if we all just... stopped.

Not in a reckless way. I'm not advocating for abandoning all planning or responsibility. But what if we could admit uncertainty without shame? What if "I don't know" became an acceptable answer? What if we could hold our plans lightly, understanding them as best guesses based on current information, subject to revision?

One of the strangest developments of modern life is that we've simultaneously become more specialized and more universally expected to have opinions on everything. We're supposed to be experts in our professional domains while also maintaining thoughtful positions on politics, culture, economics, parenting, health, ethics, and probably astrology. The cognitive load is extraordinary. Every topic immediately becomes a minefield of potential contradiction. So we pick tribes, adopt their talking points, and perform consistency.

But inside most of us is a person who, if given permission, would say: "I genuinely don't know about most of this. I have intuitions and partial information and lived experiences that point in certain directions, but I'm aware that all of this could be wrong."

That person is probably much wiser than the one we present publicly.

I've noticed that the moments in my own life when I've actually learned something significant have typically come after I've abandoned the pretense of knowing. It's not pleasant—there's a vulnerability to it, an exposure. But it opens up space for genuine understanding. When you stop defending a position, you can actually consider it. When you admit you don't know something, you become genuinely curious about it instead of just pretending to have it figured out.

This applies to self-knowledge too. How much time do we spend in a kind of self-deception about our own motivations, desires, and capacities? We tell ourselves stories about who we are—stories that usually feel like accurate descriptions when we're living inside them. I'm ambitious, or I'm not. I'm creative, or I'm practical. I'm an introvert, or I'm an extrovert. And sometimes these narratives are useful heuristics. But sometimes they're just convenient prisons. We mistake our current circumstances and habits for our nature, then spend years defending the walls.

What if you didn't know who you were? What if that was okay? What if the point was to keep discovering, keep surprising yourself?

There's something almost sacrilegious about that idea in a culture obsessed with self-optimization and authentic self-expression. We're supposed to find ourselves, develop ourselves, know ourselves. But what if the self is not a thing to be found—some fixed nugget of identity buried inside—but rather something that emerges through the process of living? What if who you are is less important than what you do?

I think about how many conversations would be different if they weren't performances. If I could say to a stranger, "I'm not actually sure what I think about that, but I'm interested in understanding it better. What's your take?" Instead of constructing a position and defending it. If professional environments allowed for actual intellectual humility instead of just the performative kind. If we could admit that we're figuring it out without that being held against us.

The fear, I think, is that admitting uncertainty is the same as admitting weakness. That if you don't have all the answers, people won't take you seriously, won't trust you, won't follow you. Maybe that's sometimes true. But I suspect the opposite is more often the case. I trust people who know what they don't know far more than people who seem to have everything figured out. The ones who claim certainty are either lying or delusional, and neither is particularly reassuring.

There's also something almost transcendent about genuinely not knowing. I've experienced it most clearly in moments of awe—standing in a landscape so vast it exceeds your ability to comprehend it, listening to music that bypasses language and logic, experiencing art that rewires your sense of what's possible. In those moments, there's no room for pretense. You're not thinking about how you appear. You're just present to something that exceeds your understanding.

What if we could access more of that—not in those rare transcendent moments, but in ordinary life?

I suspect it would change everything.

It would change how we relate to others, because we'd spend less energy managing impressions and more energy actually connecting. It would change how we approach problems, because we'd be willing to explore solutions without knowing in advance that they'll work. It would change our relationship to time, because we wouldn't be so fixated on a predetermined destination. It would change how we treat failure, because we'd recognize that learning requires experimentation and experimentation involves mistakes.

One of the most depressing things about modern life, I think, is how prematurely people seem to foreclose possibility. By a certain age—somewhere between twenty-five and thirty-five for many people—their lives have become surprisingly fixed. They've chosen their career, their partner, their geography, their identity, and now they're just executing on those choices. Their daily lives are about optimizing within predetermined parameters rather than questioning whether the parameters themselves are the right ones.

Is this inevitable? Or have we just become very skilled at talking ourselves into it?

I think about what would change if you gave yourself permission to not know what you'll be doing in five years. If you held your current circumstances as a story you're telling right now, not a permanent condition. If you understood that the person you are is still under construction, and that construction might take surprising directions.

The funny thing is, I don't think this would lead to chaos or directionlessness. Actually, the opposite. I think it would lead to better decision-making, because you'd be basing decisions on genuine insight rather than accumulated assumptions. It might lead to more risk-taking, yes, but the kinds of risks that lead to growth rather than the self-destructive kind.

And there's something liberating about not having to be right all the time. About not having to maintain consistency across all domains of your life. About not having to have an opinion on everything. About being able to say "I don't know" and having that be the end of it rather than the beginning of an apology.

Maybe I'm romanticizing this. Maybe unlimited uncertainty would be paralyzing rather than liberating. Maybe we need some structure, some narrative coherence, some sense of direction to function. Probably true.

But I'm wondering if we couldn't find a middle ground. A way of holding our plans lightly enough that we can adjust them when reality presents better options. A way of knowing ourselves flexibly enough that we can grow. A way of engaging with the world that doesn't require performing certainty.

One practical thing that might help: asking better questions. Instead of "What should I do?" maybe "What am I curious about?" Instead of "What's the right answer?" maybe "What happens if I try this?" Instead of "Who am I?" maybe "What can I do? What do I care about? What am I willing to risk for?"

Those questions don't require false certainty. They're compatible with genuine not-knowing.

I think what I'm really trying to say is this: there's a version of your life that's possible if you admit you don't have it figured out. It might not look like the version you were supposed to have. It might not match the narrative you've been telling yourself. But it might be better. More real. More alive. More genuinely yours.

The uncertainty isn't a bug. It's not a temporary condition you need to overcome. It's the fundamental texture of human existence, and the sooner you make peace with it, the sooner you can actually start living.
